turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**This is a good offer, but it is not yet compelling enough to leave a job you like. Negotiate—do not accept the initial package.**

Google’s offer averages **$552,000 per year** at target:

- Base: $235,000
- Bonus: $47,000
- Initial equity: $270,000/year averaged over four years
- **Average target TC: $552,000**

That is only **$26,000, or roughly 5%, above your current $526,000 run rate**. Over four years, assuming constant stock prices and no refreshers at either company:

- Meta run rate: approximately **$2.104 million**
- Google offer: approximately **$2.208 million**
- Difference: only **$104,000 over four years**

A 5% premium is thin compensation for switching risk when you are happy, established, and not looking.

Current self-reported Bay Area data puts median Google L6 PM compensation around **$606,000**, though benchmarks vary considerably depending on whether they include current employees, new offers, location, and accumulated refresh grants. Your $552,000 average is therefore respectable but not obviously strong for a Bay Area L6 PM. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## The most important unresolved issue: vesting schedule

Before evaluating or negotiating further, get the exact vesting schedule **in writing**.

Google new-hire grants are commonly reported as front-loaded—often **38%/32%/20%/10%**—but you should not assume your offer follows that schedule. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

If your $1.08 million grant follows 38/32/20/10, target compensation would look like:

| Year | Equity vest | Target TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |

That makes the offer excellent in years one and two, but creates a substantial cliff. Refresh grants may partially fill it, but because they are discretionary, **do not count them as guaranteed compensation**. Google itself describes equity refresh decisions as depending on modeled recommendations, performance-related inputs, and management discretion. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Your next 12 months at Meta are approximately **$476,000** based on the $200,000 vest you specified. So if Google’s first-year vest really is 38%, Google would be about **$216,000 higher in year one**. That is meaningful—but it should not obscure the four-year economics.

## What I would ask for

I would make a package-level counter of:

- **Base: $270,000**
- **New-hire equity: $1.4 million**
- **Sign-on bonus: $150,000**

This is an opening ask, not necessarily the minimum you should accept.

Why those numbers:

### Base: $270,000

The posted range topped out at $271,000. Asking for $270,000 is defensible because:

- You already make $240,000.
- You are an experienced Meta IC6.
- You were recruited rather than actively applying.
- You are happy and need a meaningful incentive to move.
- Google currently lists comparable Senior PM roles with base ranges reaching the upper $270,000s. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS&utm_source=openai))

Your current $235,000 offer is above the midpoint of the quoted range, so it is not objectively low, but it is below your existing salary and not particularly compelling for a recruited candidate.

### Equity: $1.4 million

The current $1.08 million is $270,000 per year on a simple four-year average. Raising it to $1.4 million produces $350,000 per year on average.

At a $270,000 base, 20% bonus, and $1.4 million equity grant, average target compensation becomes:

- $270,000 base
- $54,000 bonus
- $350,000 average equity
- **$674,000 average annual TC**

That is an aggressive but reasonable anchor. Recent reported Google L6 PM data is very wide, with the upper end driven largely by equity; one current dataset puts the 90th percentile near $671,000 in total compensation. ([aakashg.com](https://www.aakashg.com/google-pm-job-offer/?utm_source=openai))

### Sign-on: $150,000

A sign-on is justified by:

- The Meta equity you would leave behind.
- The risk involved in leaving a job you like.
- Uncertainty around Google refresh grants.
- The potential long-term equity cliff.
- The absence of any sign-on in the original offer.

Your $200,000 of upcoming Meta vesting is not automatically a dollar-for-dollar loss—Google’s first-year equity replaces some or all of it—but it remains useful negotiating leverage.

## A realistic landing zone

I would view the following as a good negotiated outcome:

- **Base: $255,000–$265,000**
- **Equity: $1.25–$1.35 million**
- **Sign-on: $75,000–$125,000**

For example:

- $260,000 base
- $52,000 target bonus
- $1.3 million equity, or $325,000/year averaged
- $100,000 sign-on

That gives you:

- **$637,000 average recurring target TC**
- Plus a **$100,000 one-time payment**

That is approximately a 21% recurring premium over your current $526,000 run rate, which is much more appropriate for voluntarily leaving a role you like.

As a personal decision rule—not a universal market rule—I would want roughly a **15–20% premium** to move from a good situation. For you, that means approximately **$605,000–$631,000 in average recurring target compensation**, before assigning material value to discretionary refresh grants.

## What to say

You could send this:

> I’m very excited about the team and the opportunity. At the same time, I’m happy at Meta and wasn’t actively looking, so the economics need to make the move clearly compelling.
>
> My current annual compensation is approximately $526,000, including about $250,000 in annual equity, and I have approximately $200,000 scheduled to vest over the next 12 months. As structured, the Google offer averages approximately $552,000 annually over four years before any discretionary refresh grants. That is not quite enough of a premium for me to take on the risk of leaving a role where I’m doing well.
>
> Given my current compensation, the L6 scope, and the posted salary range, I’d like to see whether the package can be adjusted to a $270,000 base, $1.4 million initial equity grant, and a $150,000 sign-on bonus. If we can get materially closer to that package, I believe we would have a path to closing.
>
> Could you also confirm the exact vesting schedule, first vest date, and the timing and vesting structure of any future refresh grants?

If you are genuinely prepared to accept at a specific package, you can strengthen it with:

> If Google can reach [your actual acceptance package], I would be prepared to sign promptly.

Only say that if it is true.

## Questions to ask before accepting

Get explicit answers to these:

1. **What is the exact new-hire GSU vesting schedule?**
2. **When is the first vest, and is there any initial cliff?**
3. **How is the number of shares determined—grant-date price, trailing average, or another method?**
4. **When would you first become eligible for a refresh?**
5. **What is the standard or modeled refresh for an L6 PM receiving a normal performance rating?**
6. **How do refresh grants vest?**
7. **Is the bonus prorated in your first year?**
8. **Is there any repayment requirement on the sign-on if you leave?**
9. **Could the offer be structured to reduce the year-three/year-four cliff?**

They may refuse to quantify refresh grants. That itself is a reason to value them conservatively.

## Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### Accept the current offer without negotiating?

**No.** You have leverage and little downside to a professional counter.

### Negotiate?

**Yes.** This is the clear next step. Your strongest points are:

- You were recruited.
- You have a strong current position.
- Your current compensation is documented.
- Google’s base is below your existing base.
- Refresh grants are not guaranteed.
- The four-year average premium is only 5%.

### Walk away?

If Google will not materially improve the offer, I would stay at Meta **unless the Google role is substantially better for your career, enjoyment, manager quality, or future promotion prospects**.

If compensation is the primary criterion, I would want the final package to reach at least approximately:

- **$600,000–$625,000 recurring four-year average target TC**, and
- Preferably some sign-on compensation.

If Google stays at $552,000 with no sign-on, you would be switching from a situation you like for a modest long-term premium and uncertain refresh economics. That is not a bad offer—but it is a weak reason to move.

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs raised to $1,280,000 (vesting over 4 years), and no sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My recommendation: **take it—if the role and manager are at least as attractive as your current situation**

The revised offer has crossed from “not enough to justify moving” to **financially compelling**. I would not walk away over the absence of a sign-on bonus.

### Revised economics

| Component | Meta current run rate | Google revised |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $240,000 |
| Target bonus | $36,000 | $48,000 |
| Annualized initial equity | $250,000 | $320,000 |
| **Annualized TC** | **$526,000** | **$608,000** |

Google is now offering:

- **$82,000 more per year**
- A **15.6% premium**
- Approximately **$328,000 more over four years**, assuming constant stock prices, target bonuses, no raises, and no refreshers at either company

At roughly $608,000 annualized, the offer is essentially at the currently reported median of approximately $606,000 for Bay Area Google L6 PMs. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

More importantly, Google increased the equity grant by exactly **$200,000** after you identified the Meta equity you would leave behind. They effectively addressed your objection—just through equity rather than cash.

## Confirm the vesting schedule

Do not sign until you have the exact schedule and first vest date in writing.

If it uses Google’s commonly reported **38%/32%/20%/10%** schedule, your target compensation would be:

| Year | Equity vesting | Base + target bonus | Target TC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $486,400 | $288,000 | **$774,400** |
| 2 | $409,600 | $288,000 | **$697,600** |
| 3 | $256,000 | $288,000 | **$544,000** |
| 4 | $128,000 | $288,000 | **$416,000** |
| **Four-year average** | **$320,000** | **$288,000** | **$608,000** |

The 38/32/20/10 schedule is commonly reported for Google grants, but alternative schedules exist, so your actual offer documents control. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

Under that schedule, your first-year Google compensation would be about **$774,000**, compared with approximately **$476,000** from Meta over your next 12 months using the $200,000 vesting figure you supplied. That is roughly **$298,000 more in year one** before considering stock-price changes.

So although you are not getting a cash sign-on, the front-loaded grant—if confirmed—more than covers the near-term transition economically.

## The real downside: the equity cliff

The principal weakness is no longer the overall offer. It is the **year-three and year-four decline**.

Without refreshers:

- Year 1: excellent
- Year 2: excellent
- Year 3: approximately equal to your Meta run rate
- Year 4: materially below it

Refreshers are supposed to help smooth that decline, but the recruiter correctly told you they are not guaranteed. Therefore, value the offer as a guaranteed four-year package—not as $608,000 plus hypothetical future refreshers.

The good news is that the package is already strong on that basis. You do **not** need refreshers to make the first four years financially favorable. They are upside and a retention mechanism, not something necessary to justify the initial move.

## When I would decline

I would still stay at Meta if any of these apply:

1. **The Google manager or organization gives you reservations.**
2. The role has materially worse scope, promotion prospects, autonomy, or work-life balance.
3. You strongly prefer Meta’s product culture and have a plausible path to IC7.
4. The actual equity schedule is unusually back-loaded or has a meaningful initial cliff.
5. You expect Meta’s future refreshes or near-term promotion to raise your compensation substantially above the $526,000 run rate.
6. You expect to remain at Google well beyond four years but are uncomfortable relying on refresh grants after the initial grant runs down.

Because you are happy at Meta, I would not move for money alone if the new job feels like a clear qualitative downgrade. A 15.6% premium is meaningful, but not enough to compensate for a bad manager or poor organizational fit.

## When I would accept

I would accept if:

- You like and trust the hiring manager.
- The scope is genuinely L6 and supports future L7 growth.
- The product area is reasonably stable and interesting.
- The vesting schedule and first vest date are acceptable.
- There are no unusual clawback or forfeiture terms.
- You are comfortable reassessing compensation around year two, when you will know what refresh grants look like.

## Should you negotiate again?

**Probably not.** They said it is their best offer after making a meaningful improvement:

- Base increased by $5,000
- Initial equity increased by $200,000
- Average annual TC increased from $552,000 to $608,000

Another hard counter is unlikely to produce much and could make the interaction needlessly adversarial. You have already negotiated successfully.

You can make one low-friction final request before signing:

> Thank you for getting the package to this level. I appreciate the team addressing the equity I’m leaving behind. Before I finalize, could you please confirm in writing the exact vesting schedule, first vest date, first refresh-eligibility cycle, and whether the first-year bonus is prorated?

If you want, you could also ask:

> Since a sign-on isn’t available, is there any flexibility on the grant start date or first vest timing?

But I would frame that as clarification or administrative flexibility, **not another ultimatum**.

## Bottom line

**On compensation, yes—I would take the revised offer.** It is about a **16% four-year premium**, is competitive for a Bay Area Google L6 PM, and likely provides substantially more compensation in the first two years.

My decision rule would be:

- **Role/manager roughly equal or better:** accept Google.
- **Role/manager noticeably worse or Meta IC7 is realistically near:** stay at Meta.
- **Still uncertain about the role itself:** do one more conversation with the hiring manager before signing, focused on expectations, team health, decision authority, and promotion trajectory.

The absence of a sign-on bonus should no longer be the deciding issue. The revised equity grant adequately solves the financial problem; the decision now comes down primarily to **role quality and career trajectory**.
